title: How a C# program works — interview

items.question: How is C# different from TypeScript at run time?
items.answer: C# compiles to Intermediate Language (IL) with Common Type System (CTS) metadata, and the Common Language Runtime (CLR) enforces types at run time. TypeScript is a compile-time checker that emits JavaScript — the engine never sees those types. A Node.js Lambda and a .NET Lambda may both receive the same JSON event, but they run on completely different hosts with different type systems.
followUps: Where does the Common Type System sit relative to the C# language?
What does dotnet build produce that tsc does not?
items.sixtySeconds: C# keeps real types in the assembly. TypeScript erases them. CLR versus V8. Same AWS event, different process and type enforcement.

items.question: Walk through source to CPU for a typical worker, including tiered JIT.
items.answer: You write .cs files. Roslyn emits IL into a .dll assembly with metadata. At run time the CLR's Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler turns each method into native machine code — tiered JIT starts with a quick compile and recompiles hot methods at higher optimization tiers. Alternatively, ReadyToRun precompiles some IL, or Native AOT compiles everything to a native binary before deployment.
followUps: How does Tiered PGO change optimization?
items.sixtySeconds: Source to IL at build. Tiered JIT quick then optimized. R2R or AOT for cold start. Warm up before benchmarking.

items.question: How do you choose the C# language version?
items.answer: It follows the Target Framework Moniker (TFM). net10.0 means C# 14 by default. Override LangVersion only when you have a deliberate reason — never use latest, because that tracks whichever compiler is installed and breaks reproducibility across build machines.
followUps: How do you print the compiler's chosen version?
items.sixtySeconds: TFM selects LangVersion. Pin the TFM, not latest. Implicit usings are auto-generated global using statements for common namespaces.

items.question: What is the entry point of a new console app?
items.answer: Top-level statements in a single file — the default dotnet new console template. The compiler synthesizes a static Main method behind the scenes. The classic form (static int Main(string[] args)) is equivalent. Only one file per project may have top-level statements. args is a string[] of command-line arguments.
followUps: Can file-based apps use Main instead of top-level statements?
What happens if you use await at the top level?
items.sixtySeconds: One entry per executable: top-level statements or explicit Main. The compiler generates the rest. args is the command-line argument array.

items.question: What is a file-based app in .NET 10, and how do ReadyToRun and Native AOT apply?
items.answer: A single .cs file you run with dotnet run file.cs — no .csproj on disk. C# 14 #: directives configure packages, properties, and SDK inline. Publish defaults toward Native AOT for native output; use PublishAot=false for reflection-heavy scripts. ReadyToRun is a middle ground — precompiled IL, faster startup, still allows most reflection.
followUps: When is R2R better than full AOT?
items.sixtySeconds: C# 14 / .NET 10: dotnet run file.cs, #: directives. AOT default on publish. R2R middle ground. Convert when it grows.

items.question: Explain using versus assembly references to someone from a Node background.
items.answer: JavaScript import loads and binds a module. C# using only shortens type names at compile time — the assembly must already be referenced via ProjectReference or PackageReference. The CLR loads assemblies from references at runtime; usings are erased and have no runtime effect. Namespaces organize types inside an assembly, not deployment units.
followUps: When do global usings cause CS0104?
items.sixtySeconds: Reference loads assembly. using shortens names only. Namespace is organizational. Not like npm import.

items.question: Your Lambda cold start is slow — JIT, ReadyToRun, or Native AOT?
items.answer: Measure cold start separately from steady state — tiered JIT pays first-compile cost on first invocation. ReadyToRun embeds precompiled native code for much IL — good when reflection is needed. Native AOT gives smallest cold start and size but requires trim-safe dependencies. Benchmark after warm-up for steady-state throughput, not first call.
followUps: What breaks with Native AOT reflection?
items.sixtySeconds: Cold start: AOT best, R2R middle, JIT slowest first call. Steady state: tiered JIT catches up. Measure both.

items.question: What is the Common Type System (CTS) and why does it matter in interviews?
items.answer: The Common Type System (CTS) defines how types are represented and verified across all .NET languages. C# int maps to System.Int32 with known size and behavior. The Common Language Runtime (CLR) uses CTS metadata to enforce casts, virtual dispatch, and garbage collection rules at run time — unlike TypeScript where types vanish after compile. When you reference a NuGet package, you are loading assemblies whose types obey the same CTS contract.
followUps: How does value type boxing relate to CTS?
Can F# and C# share the same assembly types?
items.sixtySeconds: CTS is the shared type contract for .NET. C# types become CLR metadata. Enables cross-language interop and runtime enforcement — not erased like TS.

items.question: You see CS0104 ambiguous reference after adding global usings — what happened?
items.answer: Two namespaces you imported define the same short type name — for example Timer from System.Threading and System.Timers after implicit usings. Global usings and file-scoped namespaces do not resolve ambiguity; they only shorten names. Fix with a using alias, fully qualified name, or remove the conflicting global using. This is compile-time only — no runtime effect.
followUps: Do using directives affect which assemblies load?
items.sixtySeconds: CS0104 means two imported namespaces expose the same name. Alias or qualify. Usings never load assemblies — references do.
